analysis.problem: VLAs inherit billion-parameter VLM backbones and multi-step diffusion heads that were sized for chat, so per-step cost, memory and training cost are set by the backbone rather than by the control task. The area asks how much of that backbone a manipulation policy actually needs, and how to keep the useful part while shrinking everything else.
gaps: The three sub-areas optimize different axes (parameters in 3.1, control frequency in 3.2, bits in 3.3) and almost never report on a common axis such as measured per-step latency on the target device.

Almost all results are on LIBERO, where 0.54M parameters already reach 95% (MINERVA). Architecture claims are untested in regimes where capacity matters: long-horizon, bimanual, contact-rich, or perturbed scenes (LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-PRO).
No compact architecture has been evaluated for robustness. LoopQ shows that losses invisible on nominal LIBERO reappear under perturbation, and the same is probably true of small models.

direction.title: Put every architecture on three axes: measured latency on the target device, memory, and perturbed-benchmark success
direction.bit: Architecture papers compete on parameter count and nominal LIBERO success.
direction.flip: Parameter count stopped discriminating in 2026; the open axes are measured latency per device class and success under perturbation. A compact-model leaderboard on those axes would reorder the field.
plan: Re-evaluate the released compact checkpoints (SmolVLA, Evo-1, MicroVLA-class, CoRP-class, MINERVA-class) under LIBERO-Plus with per-call latency measured on a 3090, a desktop CPU and a Jetson-class device.
Report the Pareto front of success under perturbation versus measured ms, not FLOPs.
Feed the resulting failure modes into the 3.1 microcontroller direction.
direction.claim: x > y: the ranking of compact architectures by measured latency and perturbed success differs from their ranking by parameters and nominal LIBERO.
direction.cost: Evaluation only, no training: about 2 GPU-days of rollouts.
direction.fit: vla.cpp is the natural harness because it runs these checkpoints on CPU and GPU with the same numerics.
direction.risk: A benchmark contribution, not a mechanism. Use it as the evaluation spine for the category directions below rather than as a standalone paper.

analysis.problem: Training a VLA costs thousands of GPU-hours and millions of demonstrations, and adapting one costs new data per task. The area asks how to reach the same policy with fewer demonstrations, fewer rollouts, or fewer trainable parameters.
gaps: Training recipes ignore the conditions the policy will run under: inference delay, a compute budget, stale context. Only three papers in the whole index train with simulated delay.
Everything is validated on large backbones. For compact policies, where gradients are cheap and rollouts dominate the cost, the trade-offs are different and unexplored.
Data-efficiency gains are measured by nominal success, which LIBERO-PRO shows can be memorization.

direction.title: Train for the loop you will run in: deployment conditions as training-time variables
direction.bit: Training optimizes action likelihood on demonstrations; delay, budget and staleness are inference-time problems.
direction.flip: Sample delay, compute budget and context age during training and condition the policy on them, so one checkpoint covers the deployment envelope instead of one point in it.
plan: Extend training-time action conditioning (2512.05964) and DEFLECT with a budget and a staleness variable.
Measure success across the full envelope rather than at a single operating point.
direction.claim: x > y: one envelope-conditioned policy matches specialized policies at each operating point and beats them off-nominal.
direction.cost: One compact policy per experiment, about 1 GPU-day each.
direction.fit: The envelope is exactly what a runtime controls, so the runtime can expose it as input.
direction.risk: Umbrella framing; the concrete versions are in 4.2 and 5.5.

analysis.problem: Per-step inference is dominated by visual tokens through the backbone and by iterative action decoding. The area cuts tokens, layers, denoising steps and recomputation, and decides how much of a predicted chunk to execute before re-planning.
gaps: Four knobs (token budget, depth, decoding steps, execution horizon) are tuned by four sub-areas with four separate heuristics, each reporting average FLOPs rather than the worst-case latency that sets the control rate.
Almost all methods are validated on OpenVLA or pi0, where the backbone dominates; on compact policies the vision encoder dominates and most of these methods do not apply as published.

Gating decisions (prune, skip, reuse, replan) come from the model's own attention or confidence, which the 'Gate, not the cache' paper shows is unreliable in closed loop and nobody tests under perturbation.

direction.title: One deadline, four knobs: co-schedule tokens, depth, steps and horizon under a hard per-chunk latency bound
direction.bit: Each inference accelerator is tuned in isolation and reports average savings.
direction.flip: A controller needs a worst-case bound. Treat the four knobs as one scheduling problem per chunk with a deadline, and let the runtime pick the operating point from measured timing.
plan: Instrument a compact policy with all four knobs; characterize their joint latency surface on CPU and GPU.
Learn or search a scheduler per deadline; evaluate under injected deadlines on LIBERO.
direction.claim: x > y: a jointly scheduled policy under a fixed deadline beats the best single-knob method at the same deadline.
direction.cost: Mostly evaluation; a few GPU-days.
direction.fit: The scheduler lives in the runtime.
direction.risk: Umbrella framing; the concrete mechanisms are in 5.2 and 5.5.

analysis.problem: Turn a trained VLA into a real-time control loop on robot hardware or across edge and cloud: runtimes, kernels, pipelining, KV management and fleet serving.
gaps: Only 13 papers, with no shared deployment benchmark. Each runtime reports its own models on its own hardware, and the SmolVLA export study shows that exported variants change closed-loop behaviour, not just speed.
The algorithmic accelerators in Area 5 exist as PyTorch prototypes; the gap between their claimed and realized speed-ups in a runtime is unmeasured.
Nothing runs below Jetson class. TinyVLM reaches a microcontroller for detection only.

direction.title: Close the claimed-versus-realized gap: one runtime that implements the accelerators and reports what they buy
direction.bit: Acceleration papers report FLOPs or PyTorch wall-clock on a workstation.
direction.flip: Implement the leading token-pruning, caching and quantization methods inside one runtime and report measured latency, memory, numerical equivalence and closed-loop success on three device classes.
plan: Select the top two methods from 5.1, 5.4 and 3.3; implement them in vla.cpp.
Report realized speed-up, equivalence to the PyTorch reference and LIBERO-Plus success.
direction.claim: Bounding x: realized speed-ups are a fraction of claimed ones, and the paper quantifies it per method and device.
direction.cost: Engineering time rather than GPU time.
direction.fit: This is the vla.cpp follow-up paper.
direction.risk: System paper; novelty rests on the measurement, so the protocol has to be rigorous (7.1).

analysis.problem: Decide whether an efficiency gain is real. Nominal LIBERO is saturated and hides memorization; closed-loop latency, delay and perturbation robustness must be measured together or an efficiency claim cannot be trusted.
gaps: Only seven papers, none older than October 2025. Perturbation (LIBERO-Plus), delay (TBD-VLA) and quantization (LoopQ, VLAQuantBench) are each measured alone; no benchmark sweeps them jointly.
No protocol runs the policy on the target device while the simulator runs elsewhere, so 'edge' latency numbers are never measured in the loop.
Compact policies, the ones most likely to be deployed, have never been evaluated under perturbation.

direction.title: Evaluate efficiency in the loop: perturbation times delay times budget
direction.bit: Efficiency is a latency number measured on synthetic inputs, reported next to a nominal success rate.
direction.flip: Efficiency is a closed-loop property: report success as a function of measured delay, compute budget and perturbation, with the policy running on the device it is claimed for.
plan: Build the hardware-in-the-loop harness (7.1); run compact and quantized checkpoints through it (7.2).
direction.claim: Bounding x: how much of each reported efficiency gain survives the loop.
direction.cost: Evaluation only.
direction.fit: The harness is the runtime plus a simulator bridge.
direction.risk: Benchmark contributions need breadth of models to be cited; plan for 10+ checkpoints.

analysis.problem: Build a policy small and fast enough for one GPU, a CPU or an edge board while keeping generalist-level success, by replacing the VLM backbone (Mamba, tiny VLMs, frozen encoders), the fusion (FiLM, bridge attention, resamplers) or the action head (one-shot regression, one-step flow).
gaps: The size race is closed. MINERVA reaches 95.1% LIBERO at 0.54M parameters, MicroVLA 90.2% at 12.4M, CoRP 97.0% at 48.9M. 'Smallest model above X%' is no longer a contribution.

The encoder question is contradictory. CoRP finds that freezing DINOv2 costs 19.8 points; Patch Policy wins with frozen dense patches; MINERVA trains from scratch. No controlled study separates resolution, token budget, data scale and encoder treatment.

Latency is decoupled from parameters. MicroVLA's 12.4M model is not faster than the 48.9M one; once action generation is one step, the vision encoder dominates per-step cost. No lightweight paper reports latency below workstation class.
Compact policies are evaluated in distribution only. LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-PRO show large models collapse under camera and initial-state shifts; no compact model has been tested there.
Language is nearly inert at this scale (CoRP: only LIBERO-Goal; LIBERO-Plus: models ignore instructions). A compact 'VLA' is in practice a visuomotor policy with a task ID.

direction.title: First closed-loop manipulation policy on a microcontroller
direction.bit: Compact VLAs are designed and benchmarked for workstation GPUs; 'edge' means a Threadripper or a Jetson.
direction.flip: Treat the microcontroller envelope (about 1 MB flash, 512 KB RAM, integer-only, sub-100 ms per chunk) as the design constraint and show the first manipulation policy that closes the loop there. The question becomes which pretrained visual knowledge survives distillation into a sub-500K integer encoder.
plan: Distill DINOv2 or Theia dense features into an integer encoder of at most 400K parameters at 96 to 128 px, with a hard instruction-conditioned token budget (CoRP's finding) and a one-shot regression head emitting a 16-step chunk (MINERVA and MicroVLA findings).
Quantization-aware training to INT8, export to an MCU runtime (TFLite Micro or a ggml-style integer kernel set).
Hardware-in-the-loop evaluation: LIBERO runs on the workstation, streams frames to the board over USB, the board returns chunks; report success with the real measured delay (TBD-VLA protocol).
Ablate what breaks first below 0.25M parameters, where MINERVA sees collapse: resolution, pretraining or token budget.
direction.claim: ∃x: a manipulation policy that runs closed-loop on a microcontroller-class chip at useful success, plus a bound on the smallest encoder that keeps pretrained visual knowledge.
direction.cost: Distillation plus policy training is about 3 to 5 GPU-days; everything fits one 3090.
direction.fit: Reuses the runtime expertise directly; a 15 to 50 USD board is the only extra hardware.
direction.risk: Success may collapse at MCU resolution. That result is still publishable as a bound, and the hardware-in-the-loop protocol is reusable for 7.1.

analysis.problem: Decouple semantic reasoning (a VLM at 1 to 5 Hz) from reactive control (30 to 100 Hz) so the large model's understanding reaches a high-rate controller without paying its latency every step.
gaps: No agreed interface between the systems: latents (HiRT, DP-VLA), language subgoals, rolling KV context (AHA-WAM), generated weights (HyperVLA), gated completion states (StreamVLA). No study asks which interface degrades gracefully as the slow output goes stale.

Staleness is not measured. The fast system consumes slow features that are hundreds of milliseconds old; only the cloud-edge paper in 6.2 trains explicitly for stale features, and nobody plots success against feature age.
The trigger for re-running the slow system is a fixed period or a heuristic completion gate; nothing learns when re-thinking is worth its cost.

Training is coupled (joint fine-tuning of VLM and expert) and evaluated on static scenes where the slow system rarely needs refreshing, so the benefit is not shown on the dynamic tasks that motivate the design.
The compact policies of 3.1 are never reused as the fast system, even though they are exactly the right size for it.

direction.title: Staleness-aware dual systems: train the fast controller on aged context and learn when to re-think
direction.bit: Fast-slow systems assume the slow context is fresh enough and refresh it on a fixed schedule.
direction.flip: Make staleness a first-class input: train the fast controller under a sampled distribution of context ages with the age as a feature, and derive the re-think trigger from the controller's own measured sensitivity to older context.
plan: Cache slow-system features (SmolVLA or pi0 backbone) once per demonstration frame; no backprop through the VLM.
Train a sub-50M fast controller that consumes features k steps old, with k sampled and provided as input; compare interfaces (latents, KV context, subgoal text) under the same aging protocol.
Learn the trigger: re-run the slow system when the predicted action divergence between fresh and stale context exceeds a threshold; compare with fixed-period and completion-gated baselines.
Evaluate success versus enforced slow period on LIBERO and on a dynamic-object variant.
direction.claim: x > y: an age-conditioned fast controller with a learned trigger keeps success flat up to several times the slow period at which fixed-schedule systems degrade.
direction.cost: Feature caching about 1 GPU-day; each fast-controller run a few hours on one 3090.
direction.fit: vla.cpp can run the slow model on the GPU and the fast one on CPU with real rather than simulated staleness.
direction.risk: If LIBERO scenes never change enough for staleness to matter, the dynamic variant has to carry the result.

analysis.problem: Reduce the bits and parameters of an existing VLA (quantization, pruning, distillation) so it fits edge memory and runs faster, ideally without retraining.
gaps: Quantization saves memory but rarely wall-clock time. LoopQ and VLAQuantBench measure this directly; most papers report BitOps because sub-4-bit kernels for the flow or diffusion head and for the ViT do not exist in robot runtimes.
Evaluation is open-loop or in distribution. LoopQ shows losses invisible on nominal LIBERO reappear as 1.5 to 4.3 points under paired LIBERO-Plus perturbations.
Pruning needs recovery training (GLUESTICK, RLRC, Drop-Then-Recovery); the 'training-free' claim rarely holds for the action head.

No compression method is compared across action-head types (autoregressive tokens, flow, diffusion) with one calibration protocol; the flow head is the known soft spot and W4A4 for it (HoloQ-VLA) only just started.
Quantization noise compounds along an action chunk (DyQ-VLA hints at this) but there is no model of the closed-loop effect.

direction.title: Closed-loop-aware calibration: quantize for the trajectory, not the forward pass, and realize it in a runtime
direction.bit: Post-training quantization calibrates on per-layer reconstruction error of a single forward pass.
direction.flip: Calibrate on action-chunk divergence under rollout: weight each layer's precision by its measured closed-loop sensitivity, then implement the resulting mixed-precision scheme as real kernels so the speed-up is measured rather than counted in BitOps.
plan: Estimate per-layer closed-loop sensitivity with a few hundred counterfactual LIBERO rollouts per checkpoint (perturb one layer's precision, measure chunk divergence and success).
Allocate bits with that sensitivity as the objective; compare with Hessian and activation-range criteria (HBVLA, QuantVLA, Mix-QVLA).
Implement the scheme in vla.cpp with ggml Q4 and Q8 kernels for both backbone and flow head; report measured ms on a 3090 and a CPU.
Evaluate on LIBERO plus LIBERO-Plus to test whether sensitivity-aware allocation closes LoopQ's perturbation gap.
direction.claim: x > y: sensitivity-allocated mixed precision beats uniform and Hessian allocation at equal measured latency, and the gap widens under perturbation.
direction.cost: No training; calibration and evaluation rollouts about 2 GPU-days.
direction.fit: The strongest fit with vla.cpp: nobody has paired a quantization method with a runtime that actually executes it.
direction.risk: If the flow head dominates latency, the win must come from the head kernels; keep that implementation on the critical path of the plan.

analysis.problem: Reduce the demonstration and compute cost of imitation learning: choose which data to collect or keep (curation), use unlabeled video (latent actions), decide what to predict (tokenizers, future chunks, fewer frames) and prepare the backbone (mid-training).
gaps: Curation methods (DemInf, SCIZOR, DataMIL, CUPID, SIEVE) are each validated against different baselines and datasets. There is no shared protocol, no test of whether they compose, and no evidence they help compact policies.

Latent-action pretraining (LAPA, UniVLA) is shown at 7B scale. Whether it helps sub-100M policies, where pretraining is cheapest to try, is unknown, and the field holds two contradictory results: CoRP says pretrained initialization is decisive, MINERVA trains from scratch to 95%.

Tokenizer work (FAST, ActionCodec) targets autoregressive heads. For the one-shot regression heads that win at small scale, what to predict (chunk length, frame skip, future conditioning) is only partly answered by MINERVA, FrameSkip and FOCA.
Data efficiency is never measured against robustness. Selecting for nominal success may select for memorization (LIBERO-PRO).

direction.title: Latent-action pretraining for compact policies, measured as a demonstration-count curve
direction.bit: Pretraining benefits appear at VLM scale and need action-labelled robot data.
direction.flip: Below 50M parameters pretraining is nearly free, so the question is whether video-derived latent actions buy a multiple in demonstration efficiency where it is cheapest, and whether they explain the CoRP-versus-MINERVA disagreement.
plan: Train a LAPA-style latent-action model on LIBERO and Bridge videos at small scale; pretrain a sub-50M policy on latent actions.
Fine-tune with 10, 30, 100 and all demonstrations per task; plot success versus demonstrations against scratch and against pretrained-encoder-only initialization.
Evaluate every point on LIBERO-Plus as well, to see whether pretraining buys robustness or only nominal success.
direction.claim: x > y: latent-action pretraining shifts the demonstration curve of a compact policy by a constant factor, and the shift is larger under perturbation.
direction.cost: About 1 to 2 GPU-days per curve point set; the whole study fits in two weeks on 2 x 3090.
direction.fit: Compact policies are the deployable ones, so the result feeds directly into 3.1.
direction.risk: If scratch matches pretrained at every point, the paper becomes a negative result that settles the contradiction; still useful.

analysis.problem: RL fine-tuning of a VLA is sample- and compute-hungry: rollouts are slow, rewards sparse, gradients through billion-parameter backbones and multi-step flow heads expensive. Methods cut rollouts (RIPT-VLA, PCM, ExToken), cut gradient cost (PCM, RL-VLA³, RLinf-VLA) or obtain rewards from world models or digital twins (VLA-RFT, TwinRL).
gaps: Every method assumes a large backbone. RL for compact policies, where rollouts dominate and gradients are cheap, is unexplored, although those are the policies that get deployed.
Delay is ignored except by one paper (RL for real-time VLAs); RL-tuned policies are evaluated with zero inference latency.
Reward is a success flag. Nothing optimizes inference cost as part of the reward, so adaptive-compute decisions in 5.2 stay heuristic instead of being learned from outcomes.
Nobody checks whether RL gains survive LIBERO-Plus perturbations; RL may sharpen memorization.

direction.title: Compute-aware RL: the policy chooses its own token budget and depth under a success-minus-latency reward
direction.bit: RL fine-tuning optimizes success; compute is fixed by the architecture.
direction.flip: Expose the compute knobs (visual token budget, recurrent depth, early exit) as extra discrete actions and learn them from closed-loop outcomes with a latency penalty, so the policy spends compute where it changes the result.
plan: Start from a compact policy (CoRP-class or MicroVLA-class) with a budget knob already in the architecture (hard token budget, recurrent depth).
RIPT-style leave-one-out advantages on LIBERO rollouts, reward = success minus lambda times measured ms.
Sweep lambda to trace the success-versus-latency Pareto front; compare with every fixed-budget policy and with heuristic adaptive compute (DeeR-VLA, LoopVLA).
Evaluate on LIBERO-Plus to see where the learned policy spends compute under perturbation.
direction.claim: x > y: the learned budget policy dominates every fixed budget on the success-latency front, and spends more compute precisely on perturbed episodes.
direction.cost: Policy under 50M, rollouts on CPU cores in parallel, gradients on one 3090; about 3 GPU-days.
direction.fit: Measured ms inside the reward comes from the runtime, which makes the result hardware-specific in a defensible way.
direction.risk: Sparse rewards plus a cost term can collapse to the cheapest budget; a success floor constraint handles that.

analysis.problem: Adapt a pretrained VLA to a new embodiment, task or environment with few trainable parameters and few demonstrations, without forgetting: LoRA variants, adapters, soft prompts, continual learning, test-time training.
gaps: Continual-learning methods (CLARE, LifelongVLA, the forgetting-resistance study) rest on frozen encoders, which CoRP says cost about 20 points of nominal success; nobody measures that plasticity-versus-stability price.
Test-time training (TTT-VLA, VANE) runs inside the control loop with no latency accounting and no stopping guarantee; it is validated on a handful of environments.
Cross-embodiment adaptation (X-VLA) is shown at 1B+ scale; whether compact policies can be moved across embodiments with soft prompts is open.
Adapters never reach deployment: no runtime hot-swaps them, and the latency of merged versus separate adapters on edge devices is unmeasured.

direction.title: Off-critical-path test-time adaptation: a background learner updates a small adapter while the policy acts
direction.bit: Test-time adaptation updates the policy inside the control step, so it costs latency and can destabilize the loop.
direction.flip: Run adaptation as a separate process on the robot's own recent rollouts with a self-supervised signal, and swap adapter weights only at chunk boundaries after a cheap validation (as VANE validates prompt updates). The control loop never waits for a gradient.
plan: Self-supervised objective: future-feature prediction on frozen encoder features (VANE, SLIM-0.5B style) plus action-chunk consistency across consecutive predictions.
Treat LIBERO-Plus perturbations (camera shift, lighting, background) as the 'new environment'; measure how much of the 95-to-30 drop unsupervised adaptation recovers within N episodes.
Implement the two-process design in the runtime: inference thread plus learner thread sharing adapter weights; report control-rate jitter.
Add a rollback rule: revert the adapter when validation on recent frames worsens.
direction.claim: ∃x and x > y: adaptation with zero added control latency recovers a substantial part of the perturbation drop and beats in-loop TTT at equal wall-clock.
direction.cost: Adapter under 2M parameters; each experiment under a GPU-day.
direction.fit: A two-thread design is a runtime feature; this is a paper vla.cpp can own.
direction.risk: Self-supervised signals may adapt to the perturbation without improving success; the validation gate and rollback are the safeguard and the ablation.

analysis.problem: Hundreds of visual tokens per view per step enter a transformer whose cost grows with token count, and most tokens are background. Prune or merge tokens by attention, instruction relevance, depth, temporal change or action relevance; compress reasoning chains into latents; compress history into memory.
gaps: Crowded: 38 papers, most on LIBERO or SimplerEnv with OpenVLA or pi0 at roughly half the tokens. Gains overlap and are rarely compared head to head under the same budget.

Gate reliability is untested. Pruning scores come from attention of the same model, which the 'Gate, not the cache' paper shows drifts in closed loop; no method reports results under LIBERO-Plus distractors or lighting, where background tokens suddenly matter.
Pruning happens after the vision encoder. Only ActPrune drops tokens before encoding, which is where the latency is for compact policies.
Action-JND defined an action-level tolerance for pruning but no method uses it to set the budget dynamically.
Single-frame pruning, multi-view pruning (BFA++) and history compression (FibVLA, MemoryVLA) are separate budgets; no joint accounting.

direction.title: Pre-encoder foveation driven by gripper pose and the last action, with the budget set by action tolerance
direction.bit: Token selection runs on encoded tokens using attention as the proxy for importance.
direction.flip: Decide which image patches get encoded at all, before the encoder, from signals that do not depend on the model's own attention: gripper pose, the executed action and a learned action-tolerance (JND) criterion. Savings then land where compact policies spend their time, and the gate cannot drift with the backbone.
plan: Train a tiny patch selector (under 100K parameters) that scores patches from proprioception and the previous chunk; supervise it with Action-JND labels (does dropping this patch move the action beyond tolerance) computed offline from existing checkpoints.
Encode selected patches at full resolution and the rest as a coarse summary; keep the budget dynamic via the tolerance.
Evaluate on compact policies (CoRP, MicroVLA class) where the encoder dominates; measure ms in vla.cpp on CPU.
Stress the gate under LIBERO-Plus distractors and lighting against attention-based pruners (ADP, VLA-Pruner, SpecPrune).
direction.claim: x > y: a pre-encoder selector grounded in proprioception matches attention-based pruning in distribution and beats it under perturbation at equal measured latency.
direction.cost: Offline labels from existing checkpoints plus a tiny selector: under 2 GPU-days.
direction.fit: Patch-level sparsity needs runtime support to turn into speed; that is the runtime contribution.
direction.risk: Non-rectangular patch sets break standard ViT kernels; use a fixed-size budget with gather to keep kernels dense.

analysis.problem: Not every control step needs the full network. Early exit, layer skipping, recurrent-depth refinement, mixture-of-layers, model switching between deliberative and reactive policies, and adaptive reasoning cut average compute.
gaps: Exit and skip decisions come from the model's own confidence, which is miscalibrated under distribution shift; no calibration study exists for VLAs.
Savings are reported as average FLOPs. A controller must schedule for the worst case, and worst-case latency (which sets the achievable control rate) is rarely reported.
Switching depth or model between consecutive chunks changes the action statistics and causes jerk; smoothness across transitions is unmeasured.
Budget signals are internal; none takes an external cost (thermal state, contention, battery) as input.

direction.title: Anytime VLA: exit-consistent chunks under a hard deadline
direction.bit: Adaptive-depth policies decide how deep to go from confidence and report average savings.
direction.flip: Make the policy anytime: whatever depth the deadline allows must produce a chunk that is statistically consistent with the deeper chunk, so a runtime can cut computation at an arbitrary time without a jerk. The decision moves from the model's confidence to the runtime's clock.
plan: Train a recurrent-depth or multi-exit compact policy with a cross-exit consistency loss on the predicted chunk (distribution and smoothness), not only per-exit action loss.
Add an external budget input (deadline in ms) so the policy can plan a chunk that it will have time to finish.
Evaluate with injected deadlines and delay on LIBERO (TBD-VLA protocol) and report worst-case latency, jerk at transitions and success.
Compare with DeeR-VLA, LoopVLA and model-switching (EMS) at matched worst-case latency.
direction.claim: x > y: at equal worst-case latency, an exit-consistent anytime policy beats confidence-gated early exit on success and on action smoothness.
direction.cost: Compact policy training, about 1 GPU-day per variant.
direction.fit: The runtime enforces the deadline and measures the actual cut point; the mechanism is useless without one.
direction.risk: Consistency across exits may cost nominal success at full depth; report that trade-off explicitly.

analysis.problem: Autoregressive heads need many sequential token steps and diffusion or flow heads need many denoising steps. Make the head one-shot or few-step (parallel decoding, consistency, one-step flow, speculative decoding) or compress the chunk with better tokenizers.
gaps: Near saturation at small scale: MINERVA finds flow adds nothing over regression, and One-Step VLA, SnapFlow and CF-VLA all reach near parity with multi-step heads. Where multimodality actually matters (multi-strategy demonstrations, contact-rich tasks) is not in the benchmarks.
Tokenizers (FAST, BEAST, VQ-VLA, OmniSAT, FASTer, MINT) target autoregressive backbones; there is no comparison of tokenizer against continuous head on the same backbone at equal latency.
Delay interaction is ignored. TBD-VLA shows success collapses from 97.7% to 72.3% under a 4-step delay unless real-time chunking is used; most one-step papers do not evaluate under delay.
Uncertainty costs samples. FabriVLA and KeyStone get calibration or consensus from repeated sampling, which multiplies cost; no one-shot head provides calibrated uncertainty.

direction.title: K-hypothesis one-shot heads: one pass, several candidate chunks, a learned selector, and uncertainty for free
direction.bit: Multimodal action distributions need iterative samplers; one-shot regression averages modes.
direction.flip: A single forward pass can emit K candidate chunks trained with a winner-take-all loss (multiple-choice learning) and a selector; disagreement among hypotheses is a calibrated uncertainty signal at zero extra passes, which 5.5 can use to decide the execution horizon.
plan: Build a benchmark subset where multimodality is real: LIBERO tasks re-demonstrated with two valid strategies, plus a contact-rich suite.
Train K-hypothesis heads (K = 4 to 8) on compact and mid-size policies; compare with flow (5 to 10 steps), one-step flow and plain regression at equal latency.
Use hypothesis disagreement to set the execution horizon and to trigger replanning; evaluate under injected delay.
Report calibration (does disagreement predict failure) alongside success and ms.
direction.claim: x > y: at equal latency a K-hypothesis head matches flow where modes exist and beats regression there, while providing calibrated uncertainty that improves horizon selection.
direction.cost: About 1 GPU-day per head variant on one 3090.
direction.fit: One pass, dense kernels, no sampler: the easiest head to run in a C++ runtime.
direction.risk: If the benchmarks contain no real multimodality, the head only matches regression; the multimodal subset is therefore part of the contribution.

analysis.problem: Consecutive frames are nearly identical, so reuse visual tokens, KV caches, denoising intermediates, reasoning text or whole actions across steps instead of recomputing them.
gaps: Reuse gates (pixel differences, attention entropy, action confidence) are heuristic and fail on abrupt change; the 'Gate, not the cache' paper shows the gate, not the cache, bounds reliability. RoboWorM audits world-model caching, but nothing audits VLA caches under perturbation.
Savings are measured on pi0 or OpenVLA where the backbone dominates. For compact policies the encoder dominates, and only the temporal-redundancy paper reuses computation inside the ViT.
Cache schedules are searched offline for a fixed task (EVO, BAC); no online adaptation.
Caches cost RAM on edge devices; papers report FLOPs and never memory.

direction.title: Event-driven perception: run the encoder only when a learned change detector predicts the action would change
direction.bit: Cache invalidation is decided by a proxy (pixel diff, attention entropy) tuned by hand.
direction.flip: Train the gate on the quantity that matters: whether recomputing would move the action beyond tolerance. A tiny detector on raw pixels or early ViT features predicts that label; the full encoder runs only on 'events'. This is a learned gate with the right supervision rather than a better heuristic.
plan: Generate labels offline from existing checkpoints: for consecutive frames, compute both actions and mark an event when their divergence exceeds an Action-JND tolerance.
Train a detector under 50K parameters on pixels plus proprioception; measure precision and recall of events on held-out tasks and on LIBERO-Plus dynamic distractors.
Integrate in vla.cpp: reuse cached tokens between events, report measured ms, cache RAM and control-rate jitter on CPU.
Compare with VLA-Cache, Gated VLA-Cache and temporal token reuse at equal success.
direction.claim: x > y: an action-divergence-trained gate achieves higher reuse at the same closed-loop success than proxy gates, and does not fail under perturbation where proxy gates do.
direction.cost: Label generation plus a tiny detector: under 1 GPU-day.
direction.fit: Cache management is a runtime feature; the memory accounting is a direct runtime contribution.
direction.risk: Events may be frequent on cluttered real scenes; the honest result is the reuse rate versus scene dynamics curve.

analysis.problem: Chunking amortizes one inference over k steps but delays reaction. Choose the execution horizon adaptively (entropy, kinematic phase, consensus, verifier) and handle inference delay (real-time chunking, training-time conditioning, DEFLECT, Action ControlNet).
gaps: Delay handling is crowded (RTC, training-time conditioning, DEFLECT, Action ControlNet, TBD-VLA) and each method uses its own delay model; the asynchronous-inference study is the only controlled comparison.
Horizon-selection methods are not compared against the simplest baseline, a shorter fixed horizon with a faster model, and the trade-off between horizon and inference cost saved is rarely plotted.
Every method assumes one policy cadence; no co-design with adaptive compute (5.2) or caching (5.4), even though the horizon decides how much compute is available.
Delay on real robots varies with load, and no method adapts to measured delay online.

direction.title: Horizon-compute co-scheduling from measured delay
direction.bit: Execution horizon is chosen from the policy's uncertainty, assuming a fixed inference time.
direction.flip: Choose horizon and compute budget together, per chunk, from the measured inference time and the chunk's uncertainty: a longer horizon buys compute for the next inference, a shorter one buys reactivity. A small scheduling head on a frozen policy learns this from closed-loop outcomes.
plan: Freeze a compact chunking policy with a budget knob; add a scheduling head (DEHP-style) that outputs horizon and budget from uncertainty, measured delay and proprioception.
Train by RL on LIBERO with the real timing loop from vla.cpp in place of simulated delay; reward success with a cost on reaction time.
Compare with fixed horizons, AAC, DVAC and PACE at equal CPU budget; evaluate under load variation (a concurrent process on the same CPU).
Report success, reaction time and worst-case latency.
direction.claim: x > y: co-scheduling under a fixed CPU budget beats every fixed (horizon, budget) pair and every uncertainty-only horizon rule.
direction.cost: Frozen policy, small head, CPU rollouts: about 2 GPU-days.
direction.fit: The scheduler consumes timing that only the runtime knows; this is the most runtime-native direction in the inference area.
direction.risk: Measured-delay training makes results hardware-specific; report on two devices to show the schedule transfers.

analysis.problem: Execute the policy under real timing constraints: CUDA graphs, VLM and action-expert pipelining, unified KV buffers, portable C++ runtimes (vla.cpp, Embodied.cpp, PhyAI) and edge pipelines.
gaps: No standard deployment benchmark; each runtime reports its own models and hardware. The SmolVLA export study asks for a protocol that reports latency, artifact inspection, interface constraints and closed-loop success together.
Nothing below Jetson class. No manipulation policy has closed the loop on a microcontroller or sub-1W device.
Runtimes do not realize the algorithmic accelerators from Area 5; those remain PyTorch prototypes, so the realized speed-up is unknown.
Export changes behaviour: numerical differences between PyTorch, ONNX and C++ paths change closed-loop success, and no runtime validates equivalence.

direction.title: Numerical-equivalence testing for VLA runtimes: certify that an export closes the loop like its reference
direction.bit: A runtime port is validated by matching a few output tensors on sample inputs.
direction.flip: Closed-loop behaviour diverges from tiny per-step differences (SmolVLA export study). Validate exports with a trajectory-level equivalence test: paired rollouts from identical seeds, divergence measured in action space over the chunk, with a tolerance derived from Action-JND. Make it a tool, not a one-off.
plan: Define the equivalence metric: per-chunk action divergence under paired seeds, aggregated over tasks; calibrate the tolerance with Action-JND so divergence below it provably keeps success.
Run it on vla.cpp against PyTorch for each supported model and quantization level; publish the equivalence table.
Use it to localize the layer or kernel responsible when equivalence fails (bisection over the graph).
Add it to the runtime's CI.
direction.claim: Bounding x: the equivalence test predicts closed-loop success loss from export, and a table of which kernels break it.
direction.cost: Evaluation only; about 1 GPU-day per model.
direction.fit: Directly strengthens vla.cpp and gives Area 7 a reusable tool.
direction.risk: System contribution; pair it with a mechanism paper (3.3 or 5.4) for a venue that wants novelty.

analysis.problem: Share expensive VLA inference across a fleet or split it between edge and cloud: model-hardware-aware partitioning, execution-aware scheduling that interleaves inference with motion, and edge controllers trained to tolerate stale cloud features.
gaps: Four papers only, all assuming a reliable link to a datacenter; none handles disconnection or bandwidth collapse.
The cloud-edge split keeps the semantic backbone remote; the stale-feature edge controller is the only mechanism and has no bound on tolerable staleness (shared gap with 3.2).
Fleet serving is evaluated on throughput; per-robot closed-loop success under contention is not reported.

direction.title: Graceful degradation under link loss: a staleness-conditioned edge controller with a safe local fallback
direction.bit: Edge-cloud VLAs assume the cloud feature arrives within a bounded delay.
direction.flip: Condition the edge controller on feature age and train it on recorded network traces so it degrades predictably: beyond a learned staleness threshold it switches to a compact local policy (from 3.1) rather than acting on stale semantics.
plan: Replay real WiFi and cellular traces in a LIBERO loop; the cloud backbone runs on one 3090, the edge controller on CPU.
Train the edge controller with feature age as input and a confidence head; learn the switch-over threshold from closed-loop outcomes.
Report success versus link quality against the non-blocking cloud-edge baseline and against local-only.
direction.claim: x > y: the age-conditioned controller keeps success within a few points of the connected case across trace conditions where the baseline collapses.
direction.cost: Under 2 GPU-days; mostly CPU rollouts.
direction.fit: The two-device split is the runtime's natural deployment story.
direction.risk: Shares the staleness machinery with 3.2; do them as one project with two evaluations.

analysis.problem: Nominal LIBERO scores are saturated and insensitive. Build benchmarks that perturb the scene (LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-PRO), inject inference delay (TBD-VLA), quantize in the loop (LoopQ, VLAQuantBench) and measure latency inside the control loop.
gaps: No benchmark jointly sweeps perturbation, delay and compute budget; each paper varies one.
No hardware-in-the-loop protocol: the policy and the simulator run on the same workstation, so the reported latency is never the deployed latency.
Compact policies (3.1) have never been evaluated on LIBERO-Plus or LIBERO-PRO.
Latency is measured with synthetic inputs; the SmolVLA export study shows closed-loop success and latency have to be reported together.

direction.title: LIBERO-Edge: hardware-in-the-loop evaluation with the policy on the target device and joint perturbation-delay sweeps
direction.bit: Benchmarks run policy and simulator on one workstation and vary one stressor.
direction.flip: Run the policy on the device it is claimed for (CPU, Jetson, microcontroller), bridge frames and chunks over a real link, and sweep perturbation and compute budget with the delay that actually results. The benchmark reports a surface, not a number.
plan: Simulator bridge: LIBERO on the workstation, policy on the device, frames and chunks over USB or Ethernet with timestamps.
Sweep LIBERO-Plus perturbation dimensions times device class times budget knob for 10+ released checkpoints, compact ones included.
Publish the surfaces and a single summary metric: area under success-versus-delay at a given perturbation level.
Keep the harness model-agnostic so the directions in 3.1, 5.2 and 5.5 evaluate on it.
direction.claim: Bounding x: how much nominal success survives real device delay plus perturbation, per model class.
direction.cost: Rollouts only; a few GPU-days over the study.
direction.fit: vla.cpp is the device-side runtime; the harness is the shared instrument for every other direction here.
direction.risk: Benchmark papers need adoption; release the bridge early and evaluate others' checkpoints to get cited.

analysis.problem: Understand which representation choices make a policy robust to viewpoint, lighting and distractors instead of memorizing the training camera.
gaps: Two papers, both on viewpoint. Nothing on how efficiency methods (pruning, quantization, caching, early exit) interact with robustness, although LoopQ shows quantization losses surface under perturbation.
The 'dense frozen features are more robust' hypothesis (Patch Policy, the viewpoint study) has not been tested against CoRP's fine-tuned resampler on the same perturbations.
Geometry-grounded tokens (gripper-relative conditioning) are shown for mid-size policies; whether they survive the token budgets of compact policies is open.

direction.title: Does efficiency cost robustness? A factorial study of accelerators against perturbations, then a geometry-grounded fix
direction.bit: Accelerators are validated on nominal success; robustness is a separate research line.
direction.flip: Cross every accelerator class with every perturbation dimension on the same checkpoints and find which efficiency methods are safe. The analysis predicts a mechanism: methods that drop tokens by attention fail under distractors, so grounding token selection in gripper geometry (7.2's own finding) should make pruning robust.
plan: Factorial sweep: {token pruning, 4-bit quantization, KV caching, early exit} times {camera, lighting, background, distractor, initial state} on 2 or 3 checkpoints with LIBERO-Plus.
Report the interaction table: which accelerator loses how many points under which perturbation.
Follow-up mechanism: gripper-relative token selection for a compact policy, evaluated on the same table.
Test the frozen-dense versus fine-tuned-resampler hypothesis on the same perturbations as a side result.
direction.claim: x > y and bounding x: a table of robustness costs per accelerator, and a geometry-grounded pruner that removes the largest one.
direction.cost: Evaluation plus one small training run: about 3 GPU-days.
direction.fit: The sweep is exactly the test a runtime should ship with.
direction.risk: Half the contribution is analysis; the geometry-grounded pruner is what makes it a mechanism paper.
